APPARITION / KNOWLEDGE

Choosing a treble bleed in context

A treble bleed changes a volume circuit. Its effect depends on the pickup, pots, controls and load.

In this guide
Why response changes with volume →What the bypass does →Capacitor-only and parallel RC →Compare the surrounding circuit →Understand the comparison →Choose and check →Explore on the bench →Electronics glossary →

Why response changes with volume

A passive pickup, volume control and cable form an interacting impedance network. Moving the wiper changes the source impedance presented to the cable capacitance and input load. The result can change the high-frequency voltage response as well as the output level.

What the bypass does

A treble bleed connects between volume input and wiper. A capacitor provides a frequency-dependent path around part of the volume resistance. A parallel resistor adds a resistive path and changes the effective volume-control behaviour. This is a circuit change, not a universal repair.

Capacitor-only and parallel RC

The supported PRS-style example uses 180 pF. The capacitor-only example uses 1 nF. The Duncan-style example uses 1 nF and 150 kΩ in parallel. These are existing shared circuit choices; brand names describe the convention, not measured pickup data or a guarantee for every instrument.

Compare the surrounding circuit

Pot resistance and taper, pickup electrical assumptions, cable capacitance, input resistance and control position all matter. There is no universally best network. Compare at the same volume with the same assumptions before choosing a preference.

Understand the comparison

Signal Lab models electrical voltage transfer for Modern wiring with Neck or Bridge selected. Its same-volume A/B compares the circuit against no bleed. Designer uses a full-volume reference and supports deeper network exploration. Neither models acoustic SPL, amplifier or speaker response, hearing, or perceived loudness.

Choose and check

Start with the smallest change that answers your need. Verify the input and wiper terminals, leave the casing ground separate, and compare the wiring diagram before soldering. A correct equivalent network follows the same electrical laws regardless of branding.

Explore this on the bench

Explore capacitor-only and RC networks with explicit pickup, pot and cable assumptions. Each example opens a supported starting circuit; it does not identify your actual guitar or pickup measurements.

Why volume changes can alter high-frequency response, what the bypass networks do and how to compare them without a universal recipe.

  1. Volume changes more than the level
  2. Capacitor-only: a frequency-dependent bypass
  3. Adding a resistor changes the network

  6. Wire input to wiper, then inspect

Volume changes more than the level

A passive pickup, volume pot, cable capacitance and amplifier input form an interacting impedance network. Moving the wiper changes attenuation and the impedance driving the load. As a result, rolling down can change high-frequency voltage response as well as overall output. How noticeable that is depends on the circuit and listening conditions.

A treble bleed supplies an additional path between volume signal input and wiper. In Apparition’s convention those are lug 3 and lug 2. It is not a tone capacitor wired to ground, and it does not remove the need for the pot’s normal ground connection. The same capacitor type can do a different job when connected to different nodes.

Capacitor-only: a frequency-dependent bypass

A capacitor between input and wiper provides a bypass whose impedance falls with increasing frequency. It allows more of the higher-frequency signal around part of the volume resistance. The capacitance controls how that bypass interacts with the pot and load; it does not correspond to a universal amount of preserved treble.

A network that helps at one volume setting can give an overly prominent high-frequency balance at another. Larger capacitance also extends the bypass effect further down in frequency. Evaluate several useful positions rather than accepting a pleasing full-volume comparison as evidence: at full volume there is little resistance between input and wiper for the bleed to bypass.

Adding a resistor changes the network

Common network forms
FormCircuit role
Capacitor onlyFrequency-dependent input-to-wiper bypass
Capacitor and resistor in parallelAdds a resistive bypass as well as the capacitive path
Capacitor and resistor in seriesLimits the capacitor path with series resistance

A parallel resistor is connected across the same input and wiper nodes as the capacitor. It can alter volume-control progression as well as response. A series resistor belongs in the capacitor branch and produces a different network; the two arrangements are not interchangeable just because the component values match.

The existing supported examples include 180 pF capacitor-only, 1 nF capacitor-only and 1 nF with 150 kΩ in parallel. These are comparison starting points from the existing tools, not newly invented universal recommendations. The Treble Bleed Designer provides more detailed exploration; inspect its declared topology and assumptions.

Pot taper, pickup and load still matter

A bleed network changes the effective circuit around the moving wiper, so the same components can behave differently with a different pot resistance or taper. Pickup inductance and resistance, cable capacitance and input resistance also affect the result. A recipe that works in one guitar is not evidence that it is optimal in every other guitar.

Compare like with like. Hold pickup selection, cable, input and control position constant for a circuit A/B. A matched-output listening comparison is useful too, but it answers a different question from a same-knob-position comparison. Do not confuse modelled voltage transfer with perceived loudness or the response of the complete amplifier and speaker.

Choose the smallest useful change

First decide whether you need the quieter setting to retain more high-frequency content, a different volume sweep or both. Compare no bleed with capacitor-only and RC options. Include low, middle and high volume settings and listen for an adjustment range that remains useful. There is no requirement to install a bleed in a circuit that already behaves as you want.

Network names are not pickup data

Names such as PRS-style or Duncan-style identify a familiar convention. They do not supply measured pickup parameters and do not guarantee the same result across instruments.

If the volume sweep is already the problem, changing the network can complicate diagnosis. Record the pot’s resistance and taper, establish a baseline without the bleed, then compare one network at a time.

Wire input to wiper, then inspect

Verify lug 3 as signal input and lug 2 as the wiper/output before adding the network. Physical left and right reverse with viewing orientation. Insulate exposed leads as needed and leave clearance around grounded casings and adjacent terminals. The normal output remains wiper/lug 2 → jack TIP; sleeve is the return connection.

Use the Designer to experiment, then the wiring reference for the actual supported layout. Component shopping comes after that decision: capacitance, resistance, tolerance, dimensions and assembly quality are the useful specifications. Avoid buying a network solely because a branded recipe promises to preserve an undefined perfect tone.
